title: Collections and LINQ
summary: Store data in arrays, List<T>, Dictionary<TKey,TValue> and HashSet<T>, then filter, transform, sort and aggregate it with LINQ, including deferred execution.
introduction: Real programs deal with many values at once: the lines of a file, the items in a cart, the users of a system. .NET's generic collections hold them, and LINQ (Language Integrated Query) lets you ask questions about them in a few readable lines instead of nested loops. This lesson introduces the collections you will use daily, the methods for adding, finding and removing items, and the core LINQ operators: Where, Select, OrderBy, GroupBy, aggregates and query syntax, including the deferred execution rule that trips up newcomers.
learningObjectives: Choose between arrays, List<T>, Dictionary<TKey,TValue> and HashSet<T>
Filter, project, sort and aggregate collections with LINQ methods and lambdas
Explain deferred execution and when a query actually runs

blocks.text: An **array** has a fixed length chosen when it is created and is the leanest option when the size is known. A `List<T>` grows as you add items and is the default choice for "a bunch of things". The `<T>` is a **generic type parameter**: `List<string>` holds only strings, and the compiler rejects `todo.Add(42)`. Both use zero-based indexes, `^1` means "one from the end", and `1..3` is a range covering indexes 1 and 2.

blocks.text: A `Dictionary<TKey, TValue>` maps each unique key to a value and finds it in constant time no matter how many entries it holds. Reading a key that is missing throws `KeyNotFoundException`, so use `TryGetValue` or `ContainsKey` when the key might be absent. A `HashSet<T>` is a bag of unique items; adding a duplicate is ignored and `Add` returns `false`.

blocks.text: Dictionaries do not promise an order. The insertion order you see here happens to be preserved while nothing has been removed, but never rely on it; use `SortedDictionary` or sort the keys with LINQ when order matters. The `foreach` line deconstructs each `KeyValuePair` into two variables.

LINQ adds query methods to every `IEnumerable<T>`, which includes arrays, lists, dictionaries and strings. Each method takes a **lambda expression**, an inline function written as `parameter => result`. `Where` keeps the elements for which the lambda is true, `Select` transforms each element, `OrderBy` sorts, and aggregates such as `Sum`, `Max`, `Average`, `Count`, `Any`, `All` and `First` reduce a sequence to one value. The `System.Linq` namespace is imported automatically in new projects.
Notice that `numbers` itself never changes: LINQ methods return new sequences and leave the source alone. `First` throws when nothing matches; `FirstOrDefault` returns `null` or `0` instead.

Each LINQ method returns a new sequence, so calls chain naturally into a pipeline that reads top to bottom. The same queries can be written in **query syntax** that looks like SQL; the compiler translates it into the method calls, so pick whichever reads better. `ToList()` or `ToArray()` at the end turns the result into a real collection, and `GroupBy` splits a sequence into groups with a `Key`. (`record` declares a compact data class; the [next lesson](/tutorials/csharp/properties-records) explains it.)

blocks.text: Most LINQ methods do not run when you call them. `Where` and `Select` build a *description* of the query; the work happens when something enumerates the result, such as `foreach`, `string.Join`, `ToList()` or `Count()`. That is efficient, because only the elements that are needed get produced, but it means the query sees the collection as it is *at enumeration time*, and enumerating twice runs it twice.

blocks.title: Modifying a collection while iterating it
blocks.text: Adding or removing items inside a `foreach` over a `List<T>` throws `InvalidOperationException: Collection was modified; enumeration operation may not execute.` Build a new list with `Where` (or use `RemoveAll`) instead of removing inside the loop, and because LINQ is deferred, call `ToList()` *before* you start changing the source.

blocks.title: LINQ and SQL
blocks.text: If you know SQL, `Where`, `OrderBy`, `GroupBy` and `Select` map almost one to one onto `WHERE`, `ORDER BY`, `GROUP BY` and the select list; the [SQL tutorial](/tutorials/sql) is a good companion. Entity Framework Core translates the same LINQ queries into real SQL against a database.

questions.explanation: `Where` keeps 3, 8 and 9; `Select` multiplies them by 10 to 30, 80 and 90; `First` returns the first element, 30.

questions.question: Calling list.Where(...) immediately creates a new list containing the matching items.
questions.explanation: `Where` is deferred: it returns a query that runs only when enumerated. Call `ToList()` to materialise the result.
